newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major, back from Asia, comes down to earth.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major, back from Asia, comes down to earth.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major stared into the abyss this week.
From the top of the Khyber Pass, he gazed down the gorge leading to Afghanistan and the scene of some of Britain's most bitter reversals in the heyday of its empire.

Buoyed by the adulation that greeted him at every stop of a week-long tour of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, Major flew back early to London and the brutal realities of domestic politics in the immediate run-up to a general election.

Shorn of a majority in parliament, he cut short his tour by an hour to turn up and vote late on Tuesday night for his government's finance bill. The government easily won the parliamentary vote when an opposition Labour party amendment to the bill was defeated 322 votes to 287.
But his hasty return failed to subdue him, despite the opposition Labour party's 20 point lead in opinion polls.

Making his clearest statement yet of his intention to go the distance to May 1 despite the prospect of constant parliamentary guerrilla warfare, Major told journalists: "I am prepared to play the long game."

He said the government wanted to push through key measures like its education and crime bills and the tax cuts announced in the budget -- measures which will take his government close to the May deadline for the election.
But if Major was seeking inspiration in the Khyber Pass -- the high point of a whistlestop tour through the Indian sub-continent -- the omens are not good.

Once the frontline in the 19th century's "Great Game" between the Russian Tsarist empire and the British Raj, or rule, in India, the pass has been more often the scene of heroic British defeats than dramatic victories.
The hero of its blackest day, an army surgeon called Brydon, survived against all odds to stagger into the safety of the British garrison at Jalalabad just at the edge of Major's vision.

But his heroic ride in 1842, which ended after the last of his Afghan enemies melted away when he threw his broken sword hilt at a pursuing rider in defiant despair, left behind a horrific trail of death.
Brydon was the sole survivor of more than 12,000 Britons who tried to flee Kabul.

Nervous ruling Conservative party members of parliament, surrounded by the baying hordes of opposition Labour colleagues, fear Major's determination to see his time out may indeed make him a lone hero, defiant to the last and routed through circumstance rather than a lack of personal valour.
Major is unfazed, telling reporters voters will swing back to the Conservatives when they realise that the tough economic measures taken by his government are beginning to bear fruit.

But he still faces sniping from his own side, from Eurosceptics who want him to take a tougher line against European integration, from those who feel the prime minister has gone too far to placate the Eurosceptics and from leadership contenders jockeying for position in case he falls.
The visit may, however, have given him some idea of how to deal with such rebelliousness, aides joked on the flight home.
Major was told Soviet commanders retreated from the pass in haste after tribesmen kidnapped and trussed up Soviet soldiers, before rolling them -- fatally -- back downhill to their camps.
And his guides pointed out to him the distant ruins of a building once, but no longer, used for the horrific killings of foes of the local warlords.
Captured enemies were strapped to an angled pole and slid down into a pit criss-crossed with lethal blades, chopping them into pieces.

Asked whether he fantasised about administering tribal justice to the troublesome in his fractious party, Major grinned -- and senior aides said it was hard not to reflect on what might be a fitting retribution for what they see as betrayal and rebellion in the ranks of his ruling party.
